questions.q: Why does the TickWire struct use `#pragma pack(push, 1)`?
options: It is required for every C++ struct regardless of networking use
It converts the struct's fields from integers to floating point automatically
It disables compiler-inserted padding between fields, so the struct's byte layout exactly matches what both sender and receiver agree the wire format is
It makes the struct allocate faster on the heap
questions.explain: A wire format needs an exact, predictable byte layout -- #pragma pack(push, 1) removes the compiler's normal padding so sizeof(TickWire) matches the sum of its fields precisely.

questions.q: Why does decode_tick() use the pool allocator and placement new instead of a plain `new Tick(...)` call?
options: Placement new is required by the C++ standard for all struct types
It avoids general-purpose heap allocation on every single incoming tick, which is exactly the unpredictable per-call cost Lesson 41 identified as a tail-latency risk
The pool allocator makes the Tick object immutable
Plain new is not capable of constructing structs with more than 4 fields
questions.explain: Pool allocation plus placement new is exactly Lesson 41's pattern applied here -- it removes per-tick heap allocation variance from the hot path, which matters because this loop runs on every single incoming message.

questions.q: Why does the receive loop call `release_tick()`'s explicit destructor instead of just letting the Tick object go out of scope normally?
options: release_tick() is purely cosmetic and has no functional purpose
Destructors are only needed for objects allocated with plain new
Placement new's matching cleanup is never automatic -- the destructor must be called explicitly before the slot can be safely returned to the pool's free list
Tick objects in a pool never need their destructors called
questions.explain: Because the object was constructed with placement new rather than ordinary new, there is no automatic matching delete to call its destructor -- that responsibility falls to release_tick() before the slot is reused.

questions.q: Why would using plain `new Tick(...)` instead of the pool allocator still 'work' in a quick functional test but show up as a real problem in sustained-load p99.9 latency?
options: Plain new always crashes immediately, so this scenario could never pass any functional test
p99.9 and functional correctness measure the exact same thing
The pool allocator and plain new produce identical performance characteristics in all cases

A quick functional test rarely triggers the general-purpose allocator's occasional slower-path behavior, but under sustained high-frequency allocation that variance becomes a recurring, measurable tail -- exactly what p99.9 is designed to expose
questions.explain: A small functional test rarely hits enough allocations to surface the general-purpose allocator's unpredictable tail cost; under sustained load, that cost becomes a real, recurring pattern -- which is precisely the kind of thing a mean latency number would hide but p99.9 would reveal.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a pool allocator with no latency measurement, or latency measurement with no pool allocator, would each be incomplete on their own?
options: A pool allocator without measurement would be fast but unverified; measurement without a pool allocator would only faithfully report how slow unmanaged allocation actually is -- the combination is what makes the system both fast and verifiably so
Pool allocators and latency measurement are mutually exclusive techniques that cannot be used together
Latency measurement automatically fixes any allocator performance problems it finds
Only one of the two techniques is ever necessary in a real trading system
questions.explain: The two disciplines solve different problems -- one makes the hot path fast, the other proves it is fast (and would catch it if it weren't) -- which is why the lesson treats using both together as the actual point of the exercise.
